title: Freezer Warmest Stretch
story: A restaurant's walk-in freezer logs its temperature once a minute, in °C. A food-safety rule cares about the warmest reading in every stretch of k consecutive minutes, since one warm spike matters even if the average looks fine. The inspector wants that peak for every k-minute stretch, over logs that cover whole weeks, so the report must be fast.
task: Write warmestStretches(temps, k). Return a list with one entry for each window of k consecutive readings, in order from the start: the largest value in that window. A log of n readings has n - k + 1 windows.
Aim for O(n) time in total, no matter how large k is.

examples.explanation: With k = 1 each window is one reading, so the report is the log itself.

hints: In the window [-19, -20, -17], -17 arrived last. Can -19 or -20 ever be the warmest of a later window that also contains -17?
A reading colder than (or equal to) a newer reading can never be the peak again: the newer one is warmer and stays at least as long. Throw it away for good.

Keep only readings that could still be a peak, in arrival order. They are then falling, so the front is the peak. You add at the back, drop useless readings from the back, and drop expired ones from the front. Which structure does all three in O(1)?
Use a deque of indexes. For each minute i: pop from the back while temps[back] <= temps[i], push i, then pop the front if it is i - k or older. Once i >= k - 1, record temps[front].
bruteForce: Scan each of the n - k + 1 windows for its maximum: O(n·k). With 100,000 readings and k = 50,000, that is 50,001 windows of 50,000 readings, about 2.5 billion comparisons, though neighbouring windows share all but one reading.

tests.note: window of 1: every reading is its own peak
falling: the peak leaves the window at every step
rising: every new reading is the new peak
a duplicate peak leaves while its twin stays

js: const dq = []; // indexes; their temps fall from front to back
let head = 0;  // front of the deque (avoids slow shift())
// drop readings that can never be a peak again
if (dq[head] <= i - k) head++; // the front reading left the window
py: dq = deque()  # indexes; their temps fall from front to back
# drop readings that can never be a peak again
if dq[0] <= i - k:  # the front reading left the window
walkthrough: When a warmer reading arrives, every older reading not warmer than it is useless: the new one beats it and stays longer. Throw those away. What remains, in arrival order, is falling, so the front is the peak. Readings enter at the back and can leave from either end, so a deque is the right structure. Store indexes instead of temperatures so you can tell when the front reading has left the window.
• i = 0 (-18). Push it, so the deque is 0(-18).
• i = 1 (-16). Since -18 ≤ -16, drop index 0, then push 1. The deque is 1(-16).
• i = 2 (-19). It is colder, so keep both. The deque is 1(-16), 2(-19). This is the first full window, and its peak is -16.
• i = 3 (-20). Push it, so the deque is 1(-16), 2(-19), 3(-20). Front index 1 is still inside the window (indexes 1 to 3), so the peak is -16.
• i = 4 (-17). Drop indexes 3 and 2 from the back because both are colder, then push 4. The deque is 1(-16), 4(-17). The front index 1 equals 4 - 3, so it has expired and is dropped. The peak is -17.
• i = 5 (-21). Push it, so the deque is 4(-17), 5(-21), and the peak is -17.
In each step, clean the back first, then push, then check the front. Checking the front against i - k keeps exactly the last k minutes.
solution.timeWhy: Each index enters the deque once and leaves it at most once, from one end or the other.
solution.spaceWhy: The deque only ever holds indexes from the current window.
solution.takeaway: For the max (or min) of every sliding window, keep a monotonic deque: drop items from the back that can never win again, drop expired items from the front, and read the answer at the front. It is the monotonic stack idea with a second exit for items that age out.
